newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia signals continued tight money policy.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia signals continued tight money policy.

text.p: The Malaysian central bank's recent bills tender shows its determination to keep monetary policy tight, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday.
The one billion ringgit ($403 million) Bank Negara tender, held on Tuesday, has caused interbank rates to rise since late last week when it was first announced.
"They (the central bank) are reiterating their stand that interest rates will not drop so soon," said a dealer at a Malaysian bank.
A recent inflow of offshore money and the return of funds following the end of local annual holidays and festivities had been expected to put downward pressure on rates.
The Bank Negara tender consisted of 500 million ringgit in 91-day bills and another 500 million ringgit 30-day bills. Payment will be on Wednesday,
The Bank announced on Tuesday it had accepted yields at an average 6.343 percent in the issue of the 91-day bills. It also accepted 6.439 percent average yield for its 30-day bills.
On Tuesday, the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur interbank offered rate (Klibor) rose moderately to 7.40/45 percent from 7.35/40 on Monday.
Dealers said interbank rates -- interest rates which banks charge one another on loans -- could have slipped without the new issue as liquidity levels have been steadily rising in recent weeks.

Some three billion ringgit were expected to return slowly to the banking system from late last month after festivals in early February. Retail consumers had withdrawn money for mid-February Moslem Eid al-Fitr and Chinese Lunar New Year celebrations.
Malaysia also continues to attract offshore funds due to its relatively high interest rates, appreciating currency and strengthening economy, analysts said.
"I think Bank Negara wants to keep the rates from coming down. The money coming back into the system will be taken up by the issue," said a dealer at a large Malaysian bank.
Some dealers said the tender also reflected Bank Negara's (BN) attempt to raise yields on liquid assets held by banks.
"The yields on Treasury bills and BN bills are low. The issue will help the yields be more reflective of interbank rates," said a dealer at another bank.
The central bank maintained a tight monetary stance last year as it battled to curb inflation in a national economy which expanded by 8.2 percent.

With the economy forecast to grow a little slower at 8.0 percent this year, and with Malaysia's once-worrisome external trade balance showing improvement, some economists said the central bank could afford to ease rates in coming months.
Gyrations in three-month interbank rates directly affect Malaysian commercial interest rates.
Bank Negara calculates the base lending rate -- the rate banks offer to their top clients for loans -- by a formula which is pegged to a monthly average of the three-month interbank rate.
The three-month interbank rate's weighted average for February stood at 7.36 percent.
